transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO, Stellar Quant), Marko Vasile (Head of ML Ops), Nina Park (Finance)

Summary:
Redwood AE/SE introduced platform options (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). Main focus was on unit economics: per-token pricing, batching and KV cache levers, and how those translate to forecasted monthly spend. Stellar Quant shared constraints: 99th pct latency targets for inference, heavy batch offline jobs, and a tight budget for pilot. Agreed next steps: send pricing model, run a short benchmark on sample workload, share security docs.

Topics:
- Per-token pricing and example math
- Batching, caching (KV cache) and quantization effects on cost
- Hosted vs Dedicated tradeoffs for budget predictability
- Security/compliance (KMS, SOC2) and private options
- Pilot/benchmark scope and timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — uh — appreciate you making time, we'll keep this focused on cost economics and how Redwood maps to your stack. quick intros?
[00:08] Lena: Hi, Lena here, CTO at Stellar Quant. We run quant models and a lot of downstream NLP — chat assistants for traders and summarization pipelines.
[00:15] Marko: Marko, ML Ops. I handle deployments and infra.
[00:18] Nina: Nina from Finance, I'll be helping with procurement and budget.
[00:22] Maya: Great. Samir is our solutions engineer, he'll cover technical levers. Samir?
[00:26] Samir: Yep thanks. so high level — Redwood offers hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, and private (VPC/on-prem). For cost talk the important knobs are per-token price, batching, KV cache/prefix caching, and quantization profiles. We'll show examples.
[00:40] Marko: Quick context — our traffic profile is around 120k reqs/day, mix of short chat turns (avg seq len ~80 tokens) and longer summarization (up to 1,200 tokens). We need p95 latency under 400ms for chat. Budget for pilot is about $8k/month.
[01:02] Maya: OK that helps. two quick clarifications — are these online requests or mostly async batch jobs?
[01:07] Marko: Both: roughly 70% online low-latency, 30% bulk batch scoring overnight.
[01:12] Samir: That split matters — batching for overnight can drastically lower unit cost, but for online we rely on small-batch latency optimizations and caching. Also prefix/KV cache helps when many requests share context, for example repeated document prefixes.
[01:27] Lena: Can you give a concrete per-token example? We need to model worst-case and expected-case spend.
[01:31] Samir: Sure. Example: hosted LLM on Redwood — per-token generation price is $0.0008/token for the base open model (example), embeddings at $0.0004/unit — these are illustrative, we'll send exact sheet. If your avg chat is 80 tokens output and 50 tokens input, that's 130 tokens per call so about $0.104 per call at that rate — oh wait math: 130 * 0.0008 = 0.104, yes. *But* with batching and KV cache we can reduce effective tokens processed on GPU per request.
[02:05] Nina: That seems high — at 120k reqs/day that's like 12.5k/day? sorry — math, wait.
[02:11] Marko: 120k reqs/day * 130 tokens * 0.0008 = ~12,480/day => ~ $374k/month, that's way over our budget. So we need to see what real numbers look like with batch/caching.
[02:25] Maya: Right — the raw per-token multiply is a ceiling. Two big levers: 1) Dedicated reserved capacity reduces price per token and gives predictable throughput (committed monthly price + lower per-token), and 2) KV/prefix caching and request batching reduce GPU work. For example, with caching we might only decode new tokens for a lot of requests, reducing average tokens per request down to, say, 30 effective tokens. For your batch jobs, we can run very large batches that push unit costs low.
[02:55] Samir: Also quantization — if you can tolerate quantized weights (like 4-bit or 8-bit), you get ~x2-3 throughput on certain GPUs which lowers footprint, but you must evaluate quality delta.
[03:07] Lena: The caching example — is that something Redwood manages transparently or do we have to change code?
[03:12] Samir: We provide automatic KV cache for chat-style workloads and prefix caching for repeated prompts. There are SDK calls to control TTLs and cache keys. Some engineering to wire it up if you use custom prompts, but it's fairly straightforward. We've seen customers cut token cost by 40-70% depending on reuse.
[03:29] Marko: For our summarization pipelines there's less reuse, though the batch jobs are pure offline so good candidates for Dedicated. Can you quantify dedicated committed pricing?
[03:37] Maya: High level: dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and a much lower per-token compute rate; also you get predictable throughput. The pricing depends on GPU type and commit length — monthly commit vs yearly. Example: on A10-like equivalent you might see ~30-40% reduction in per-token vs hosted; on H100-equivalent it's different. We'll include ranges in the pricing sheet.
[03:58] Nina: What's the minimum commit? Our procurement needs a predictable monthly number.
[04:02] Maya: Typical entry is a smallest dedicated pool for pilot — we'll propose a three-month reserved pilot that matches your batch windows. If procurement needs a cap we can model scenarios: hosted with budget alerts, or dedicated with commit.
[04:12] Samir: Another angle is hybrid routing — keep online low-latency on hosted for burst and use dedicated for steady throughput; Redwood supports routing policies and automated fallback. That gives both predictability and cost control.
[04:26] Marko: On the latency front — you mentioned p95 400ms target earlier. For hosted we can hit sub-200ms for short chats on optimized kernels; for dedicated it depends on hardware and model size. We should run a benchmark with your actual prompts to validate p95.
[04:41] Lena: Agreed. Also security: we need SOC2, SSO (SAML), audit logs, and KMS for keys. Private deployment maybe required for certain clients with restricted data.
[04:50] Maya: We can share SOC2 and ISO reports, and we support SAML SSO + RBAC + KMS integrations. Private (VPC/on-prem) is possible if you need full control; that has different pricing/ops implications. We'll attach docs.
[04:59] Nina: If we go dedicated, how does data residency/audit work — do you ship logs to our SIEM or can we keep logs in our VPC?
[05:06] Samir: In dedicated/private setups you can forward logs to your SIEM or keep logs in your VPC; we also offer long-term audit retention as an add-on.
[05:12] Marko: One practical question — for our overnight batch scoring, what's the best way to minimize cost? Larger batching and lower-precision models?
[05:18] Samir: Exactly. For batch scoring you pick a model variant that balances quality and throughput, apply quantization where acceptable, and run heavy batch windows at off-peak times — with large continuous batches GPU occupancy is high and tokens per second cost plummets. You can also use cheaper instance types for batch.
[05:31] Lena: Are there any hard limits on concurrency or queueing that would affect our online SLAs?
[05:35] Samir: We expose queuing metrics and autoscaling policies; on hosted you have quotas but we can set higher limits for enterprise customers. Dedicated gives you the capacity you reserve, so less noisy neighbors.
[05:45] Nina: Back to numbers — can we do a quick back-of-envelope if caching cuts tokens by 50% and dedicated reduces per-token by 35%? With initial raw $0.0008/token.
[05:55] Samir: Sure. Raw: 130 tokens * 0.0008 = $0.104 per call. If caching reduces effective tokens to 65 tokens that's $0.052. Dedicated reduces per-token to ~0.00052 (35% lower) => 65 * 0.00052 = $0.0338 per call. At 120k/day => 3,960/day => ~$120k/month. Still above $8k but much closer depending on further batching for parts of workload and model choice.
[06:22] Marko: So still high — we need to consider model selection (smaller model for chats), aggressive caching, and routing heuristics. Could you recommend model variants?
[06:30] Samir: Yes, we maintain a model catalog with recommended variants per workload. For short chat you can often use a smaller LLM with instruction tuning; for longer summarization you may pick a higher-capacity variant for best quality. We'll propose specific candidates after we see sample prompts.
[06:46] Lena: What's the pilot scope you recommend given our $8k/month pilot budget?
[06:50] Maya: For $8k/month, we recommend a focused pilot: 2-week dedicated micro-pool for batch scoring (to prove unit cost reduction) plus hosted for online chat with heavy caching enabled. The goal is to demonstrate a 30-50% reduction in unit costs for the batch portion and validate latency for online.
[07:06] Nina: Procurement timeline — we can sign a short MSA for pilot, but need clear SOW. Can you provide pricing rounded and a one-pager for procurement?
[07:14] Maya: Absolutely, we'll send a pilot SOW template and a pricing one-pager.
[07:18] Marko: A couple of notes — we'll need the benchmark runbook (metrics to collect: tokens processed, GPU utilization, p50/p95/p99 latency, cost breakdown). Also we want to test prefix caching effectiveness for our chat flows.
[07:29] Samir: We'll include a runbook and instrumentation plan. We usually instrument per-route token counts and cache hit rates so you can attribute savings.
[07:36] Lena: Any friction in integrating KMS for our keys? We use AWS KMS.
[07:40] Samir: We integrate with AWS KMS/HSMs; for private deployments you can bring your own keys. We'll send the integration guide.
[07:47] Maya: Quick note on hidden costs — networking egress for large batch results, long-term audit retention, and extra observability retention are add-ons. We'll call them out in the pricing sheet.
[07:58] Marko: One more — can Redwood support scheduled autoscaling for predictable nightly batch runs?
[08:03] Samir: Yes, dedicated pools can have scheduled scaling policies; hosted can too to an extent. We'll include suggested autoscaling config in the runbook.
[08:12] Nina: Ok, sounds good. Next steps recap?
[08:15] Maya: Recap: 1) We'll send pricing + cost model spreadsheet, 2) Samir will send benchmark plan, 3) Marko to share sample prompts and seq length hist, 4) We'll share SOC2/ISO and KMS docs, 5) Schedule follow-up for 2026-03-10 for infra deep-dive.
[08:32] Lena: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[08:35] Maya: Thanks — talk soon.
